extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters (local-news and feature writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplar pieces for writing local-market reports, short human-interest vignettes, and small-features — showing what to include (prices, sources, scenes, dialogue, logistics) and how to structure such items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report seasonal supplies and origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Current supplies of peaches are coming from widely separated points. Few California peaches are now offered, and most of the Georgia crop has also been marketed, but West Virginia, Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut are shipping freely to this market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify where produce or goods are coming from (geographic sources, e.g., states, provinces, countries). Note shifts in supply over the season and how competing origins affect availability and price (e.g., Connecticut freight advantage over New Jersey). Use origin information to explain price/quality differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish wholesale vs retail prices and margins
rubrics_metrics.description: Wholesale prices are reasonable, as usual when the crop is large, but prices at retail rarely fall below a certain level. Wholesalers say that the retailers are to blame, and the latter say that they cannot afford to handle the fruit except with a generous margin of profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both wholesale and retail figures and, when relevant, discuss margins and the perspectives of wholesalers, retailers, and consumers. Explain why wholesale abundance may not translate into low retail prices (transport, handling, retailer margins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give concrete unit prices, package types and grades
rubrics_metrics.description: By the dozen, good peaches can be bought for 10 to 25 cents. The small baskets that come in the carriers bring 40 to 50 cents, while old-fashioned peach baskets sell at 75 cents to $1.25. Green corn is selling at 20 to 25 cents a dozen ears; tomatoes at 8 to 10 cents a pound; native roasting chickens are selling at 35 cents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific prices with the unit (per dozen, per basket, per peck, per pound, per pair) and, where applicable, separate by grade/cut/origin (e.g., northern vs western, choice cuts vs others). This precision lets readers compare and decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include comparative stock/inventory statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Total stocks in local cold storage warehouses at last report were 300,191 packages, against 299,020 packages a week ago and 321,303 packages a year ago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite inventories or stocks and compare them to recent (week-ago) and year-ago figures to show trends. Use such comparisons to contextualize price movements and supply expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain transport/handling costs when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Freights and packing cost the New Jersey farmer about 50 cents for an ordinary peach basket, and more for a six-basket carrier, which is now the favorite way of shipping fine table fruit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When price differences hinge on distance or packaging, give freight/packing cost figures and describe packaging types (baskets, carriers). This clarifies producers' margins and competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe varieties and quality attributes; advise buyers
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, early peaches are clingstones and late peaches are freestones. The latter have manifest advantages, but when they are desired care should be taken to see that the buyer gets what is wanted. Sweetness and flavor should also be insisted upon, while it is always a mistake to buy half-rotten fruit because it is cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note varietal differences (e.g., clingstone vs freestone), seasonal characteristics, and sensory quality (sweetness, flavor, firmness). Offer practical buying advice and warn against obvious anti-patterns (buying half-rotten fruit for low price).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid scene-setting, dialogue and local color in short vignettes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a clerk at the desk of Bretton Hall picked up the desk telephone... 'If they's such a thing as a bootjack in this metropolitan hostlery,' a co'n and cotton voice enunciated in exasperated accents... 'By gad, suh!' he shouted, pounding the desk and leaning across it to glare at the astonished clerk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a concrete scene or exchange, include direct quotes (even dialect when appropriate) to characterize people, and use small dramatic details (a phone ring, a clerk's action) to bring the episode to life. Short human-interest items thrive on immediacy and recognizable moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture recurring-routine characters and small human gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Wake up! Your station next,' shouted the Subway guard... 'I have awakened him so regularly that he thinks now it is one of my duties.' 'We know practically all the regular passengers on the late night trains.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For brief local sketches, highlight routines, recurring characters, and small acts of service or habit that reveal community and human relationships. These details give readers a sense of place and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure feature narratives with prologue, time-jump and payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: [Curtain] ... Alack, never again did man set eyes on the Good Faith. ... [Stars here indicate hiatus of 220 years.] ... A fisher of sponges ... looked over the side ... he came up with pieces of eight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a historical prologue or evocative opening to establish stakes, then jump forward to the modern discovery; build suspense and provide a satisfying payoff (discovery, legal complication, plot). Explicitly marking hiatuses (e.g., 'stars indicate hiatus of 220 years') helps structure long-form local adventure features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface narratives with named characters, credentials and authority details
rubrics_metrics.description: Skipper Scull, Harvard, '98 ... Gordon Brown, Yale, '01 ... Roger Darby, Harvard, '05 ... Alexander Forbes, the grandson of John Murray Forbes, is the possessor of the yacht Merlin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List key participants with identifying details (names, affiliations, credentials, family background) to lend authority and color. Such specifics help readers judge competence, motive and social texture of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report logistics, routes, hazards and probable outcomes for expedition stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a few weeks the Cluett will be feeling out open reaches in the ice which is rarely absent after Nachvak Bay, on the north Labrador coast, laying a course almost due north up Davis Strait... The diminutive wooden sailing ship ... will then find herself encompassed with leagues of ice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering relief or exploration missions, include the vessel, route, seasonal hazards (ice, weather), supplies on board, timelines, and realistic expectations of success or delay. These details inform readers about risk and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an engaging tone: mix romance, humor and local consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance lies behind the horizon and the glint of the rising sun has the glint of Sir Henry's gold... 'Of course the ship was searched, but Abraham was missing.' 'Yesterday the Hebrew's daring act was talked of admiringly in many quarters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an engaging narrative voice that can oscillate between playful/romantic and factual/local consequence. Using evocative language (romance, mystery) is acceptable in feature pieces so long as factual anchors remain (names, dates, prices, outcomes). Avoid sensationalism that obscures core facts.
